title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general method for building public-key encryption from any one-way function. A one-way function is efficient to compute but hard to invert on randomly generated inputs. Public-key encryption would let someone publish an encryption key that anyone can use, while keeping a secret decryption key. The target is a construction in the plain model, with polynomial-time algorithms and a proof that breaking the encryption would yield an efficient way to invert the underlying function. This is the proposed capability, not a construction demonstrated by the supplied material.

The central distinction is between ordinary public-key security and a limited computational advantage over an attacker. The supplied review documents an article describing fine-grained key agreement from exponentially hard one-way functions, where the attacker needs only polynomially more computation than the legitimate participants. CRY-02 seeks ordinary encryption security against every probabilistic polynomial-time attacker under the general one-way-function assumption. Interactive key agreement is a related capability, but achieving it would not by itself establish the public-key encryption construction sought here.

significance.text: If achieved, the construction would establish public-key encryption under the same general assumption that supports much symmetric cryptography. The reviewed article describes one-way functions as supporting capabilities including stream ciphers and pseudorandom functions, alongside digital signatures. Extending that foundation to public-key encryption would resolve a basic question about which cryptographic capabilities follow from one-wayness. The revolutionary significance is this theoretical implication; the supplied evidence does not predict that such a construction will succeed.

The immediate consequence would be a security reduction: an efficient successful attack on the encryption scheme could be converted into an efficient inverter for its underlying one-way function. As a conditional downstream possibility, a sufficiently efficient construction could broaden the foundations available for practical public-key systems. However, an asymptotic implication would not automatically preserve a named symmetric primitive’s concrete security, produce elliptic-curve-sized keys, or deliver competitive runtime and bandwidth. Those outcomes would require separate instantiation, parameter analysis, and engineering.

The fine-grained comparison explains the size of the conceptual advance. Even exponentially hard one-way functions are reported to support key agreement with only a polynomial security gap in the documented benchmark. Ordinary public-key encryption from an ordinary one-way function would instead have to resist all polynomial-time adversaries. A quadratic attacker-versus-participant work gap can be meaningful in a bounded setting, but it does not supply that ordinary asymptotic guarantee.

The impact should not be justified by asserting an established plain-model separation between one-way functions and public-key cryptography. The reviewed article discusses black-box or oracle separations, which constrain particular proof frameworks or describe relativized settings. They do not, by themselves, prove that one-way functions can exist without public-key encryption in the unrestricted plain model.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a general way to turn inversion hardness into the public-key/secret-key structure needed for encryption, together with a security proof using only the underlying function’s one-wayness. The construction must provide efficient key generation, encryption, and reliable decryption, while making the published key safe to expose. Strengthening the assumption to exponential hardness or proving only a fixed polynomial work gap would change the target rather than complete it.

A major methodological obstacle is the landscape of oracle and black-box separations discussed in the reviewed article. Any proposed construction and reduction must specify how they use the underlying function and the attacker, and explain why the applicable separation results do not rule them out. A relativization barrier alone does not establish that the construction must inspect the function’s code: restrictions on the construction and on the security reduction must be distinguished.

The research cites Impagliazzo and Rudich’s 1989 work, Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations, as a barrier to relativizing proofs of secret exchange from one-way permutations. The supplied review had no retained artifact for that source, so its exact theorem and restrictions remain unverified here. This limits how specifically the barrier can be stated; it is not evidence that the cited result is false.

An impossibility result could clarify the boundary, but its conclusion would depend on its scope. Excluding a specified class of constructions or reductions, even one encompassing some non-black-box techniques, would delimit that class. It would not automatically settle every possible implication from one-way functions to public-key encryption. Resolving the positive target requires the general construction; an unrestricted negative resolution would require a correspondingly comprehensive argument.

current_state.text: The strongest positive comparison documented in the supplied review is fine-grained key agreement from exponentially hard one-way functions. Brzuska and Couteau’s On Building Fine-Grained One-Way Functions from Strong Average-Case Hardness, published online in December 2024, discusses a Merkle-style key-agreement result with a quadratic work gap and attributes the relaxation from an ideal one-way function to exponentially hard one-way functions to Biham, Goren, and Ishai. The December 2024 article therefore documents this result; the supplied material does not establish that it originated it. The quadratic gap is a partial capability, not ordinary public-key encryption.

The same article discusses stronger hardness properties, including non-amortizability, as ways to circumvent other black-box impossibilities. This supplies context for how additional assumptions can change what is constructible. It does not substantiate the research’s specific assertion that garbling has bypassed relevant barriers, nor does it demonstrate ordinary public-key encryption from an arbitrary one-way function.

The supplied review relied on a partial extraction of the Springer article. Both indexed HTML and PDF extractions were truncated at 120,000 characters, and the separation diagram itself was not inspected, although its caption was available. These limitations allow the specific introductory comparisons above to be retained, but do not support treating the supplied record as a complete examination of the article or its separation landscape.

No supplied result demonstrates the full CRY-02 construction. Whether the target remained open on November 1, 2026 is not independently established by these inputs: the freshness-search record is empty, and the 1989 ACM source was not captured. Accordingly, the dated positive result can be reported, while the broader assertions that the historical barrier remains unchanged and that no later construction exists must remain unverified.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed theoretical completion: provide a construction for an arbitrary underlying one-way function, with a precisely specified interface and plain-model polynomial-time key-generation, encryption, and decryption algorithms. Establish correctness with negligible decryption error over the scheme’s stated message space. For every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary with non-negligible IND-CPA advantage, provide a polynomial-time inverter for the underlying function, with quantitatively specified polynomial loss. IND-CPA means that an attacker allowed to obtain encryptions cannot efficiently distinguish encryptions of its chosen equal-length messages. These are proposed acceptance criteria for this record.
completion_criteria.label: Plain-model encryption from arbitrary one-way functions with IND-CPA security reduction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed proof and reproducibility requirements: state all assumptions, randomness, parameter dependencies, message-length limits, and models of access to the function and adversary. Make the algorithms and reduction sufficiently explicit for independent checking, and explain their relationship to relevant impossibility results. A theorem is needed to justify the claim for arbitrary one-way functions. Implementations and finite tests would establish demonstrated behavior and breadth across tested instances, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independently checkable universality theorem with explicit assumptions and reduction

completion_criteria.text: A Merkle-style protocol with only a quadratic work gap would not meet the theoretical criterion, even if it performed well at selected parameters. The documented fine-grained benchmark uses a stronger hardness assumption and provides a polynomial gap. Likewise, an interactive key-agreement construction alone would leave the stated public-key encryption target unresolved.
completion_criteria.label: Full theoretical security beyond quadratic-gap protocols and interactive key agreement

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical milestone, separate from theoretical completion: instantiate the construction with a named symmetric primitive, justify a concrete 128-bit security estimate using the reduction and relevant attack costs, and measure key generation, encryption, and decryption runtimes. Test public keys and ciphertexts below 1 KB for an explicitly specified message length, reporting any setup material and additional communication. The 128-bit and 1 KB targets are optional benchmarks proposed here, not established standards, demonstrated feasibility, or necessary conditions for resolving the theoretical question.
completion_criteria.label: 128-bit instantiation with sub-1-KB public keys, ciphertexts, and runtime measurements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — CRY-01, A proof that an explicit one-way function exists, concerns establishing a foundation that CRY-02 takes as an assumption. CRY-02 asks what can be constructed from that foundation. A successful implication would not itself prove that one-way functions exist. The supplied unsolved-problems list presents one-way-function existence and public-key cryptography as separate questions, supporting their conceptual distinction without proving a separation.

Roster-based synthesis — CRY-03, Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation, concerns hiding program implementations while preserving functionality; CRY-02 concerns deriving encryption from a minimal general hardness assumption. Non-black-box techniques make the subjects methodologically adjacent, but the supplied evidence establishes no construction connecting these particular targets. CRY-04, General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost, instead concerns computing on private inputs efficiently. An encryption foundation could be relevant to such systems, but would not by itself supply general private computation or its proposed cost profile.

Roster-based synthesis — CRY-05, Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs, adds public verification and resistance to copying, properties not supplied merely by public-key encryption. CRY-06, Practical classical verification of quantum computation, concerns checking a quantum computation’s correctness. CRY-07, Position verification that works in physical spacetime, concerns authenticating location under physical and adversarial constraints. These entries share cryptographic concerns about what an adversary can accomplish, but each requires capabilities and security definitions beyond the CRY-02 encryption target.

Roster-based synthesis — CRY-08, Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost, could use public-key encryption for message confidentiality, but hiding communication relationships, timing, or routing information requires additional mechanisms. CRY-09, Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem, requires a justified delay and resistance to quantum attack; neither follows from the proposed ordinary one-way-function implication. CRY-10, A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption, evaluates particular deployed assumptions against quantum computation, whereas CRY-02 seeks a general construction from one-wayness. The proposed CRY-02 criteria address ordinary probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries; quantum security would require a separately specified assumption and proof.

brief.title: Encryption from any hard-to-reverse calculation
possible: You could publish a key that anyone could use to send you encrypted messages, while keeping the key that unlocks them secret. The new capability would be building this from any one-way function: a calculation that is easy to perform but hard to reverse on random inputs.
why: This would give public-key encryption—the published-key arrangement—the same general foundation that already supports much encryption with shared secret keys. For cryptographers, it would settle a basic question about what follows from difficulty reversing a calculation.
The proof would connect successful attacks directly to that foundation: an efficient way to break the encryption would also provide an efficient way to reverse the underlying function.

sources.showed: They proved that a strong assumption about difficulty finding patterns yields functions with a limited gap between the effort to compute and reverse them. They also describe earlier work letting people agree on a secret under stronger assumptions, with a limited advantage over attackers.
sources.quote: We show that this (very strong) average-case hardness notion already gets us outside of Pessiland: if there is a block-finding hard language, then there exists fine-grained one-way functions (with a quadratic hardness gap).
sources.cited_for: The work explains partial capabilities and limits on certain proof methods.
sources.not_established: It does not construct ordinary public-key encryption from an arbitrary one-way function.

sources.showed: Their list presents the existence of one-way functions and the possibility of public-key cryptography as separate open questions.
sources.cited_for: Assuming one-way functions exist differs from proving that they exist.
sources.not_established: Listing separate questions does not prove that their answers can differ.

sources.showed: This is theoretical work on limits to certain proofs for exchanging secrets from one-way permutations, which are reversible mappings whose inverses are hard to compute.
sources.cited_for: The work concerns barriers to particular ways of proving that secret exchange follows from hard-to-reverse mappings.
sources.not_established: A barrier to a class of proofs does not rule out every possible construction.

shown: Biham, Goren and Ishai established a related, weaker capability: people can agree on a secret using functions assumed much harder to reverse than ordinary one-way functions. The attacker must do roughly the square of the participants’ work. Brzuska and Couteau describe this result.

That advantage falls short of the target. Public-key encryption would need to withstand every attack whose running time grows polynomially—a fixed-power relationship—with the security parameter that controls the scheme’s strength.
missing: The target requires a general construction that turns any one-way function into published and secret encryption keys.
The construction needs efficient key creation, encryption and reliable decryption, with a proof connecting attacks to reversing the function.
A practical version needs concrete security analysis, compact keys and encrypted messages, and measured running times.

milestones.label: Secure encryption from any one-way function
milestones.explanation: Efficient algorithms without idealized extra tools would have to decrypt reliably and turn any efficient attack distinguishing chosen messages into an efficient function inverter. This would establish the theoretical capability.

milestones.label: An independently checkable proof covering every eligible function
milestones.explanation: A theorem would have to spell out the algorithms, assumptions, randomness, message limits and proof, including how known barriers apply. This would justify the general claim beyond tested examples.

milestones.label: Full encryption security beyond limited work advantages
milestones.explanation: The result would have to provide public-key encryption secure against every efficient attacker, beyond a fixed work advantage or an interactive agreement on a secret. This would establish the required strength and capability.

milestones.label: A practical version with justified 128-bit security
milestones.explanation: An implementation using a named shared-key building block would have to justify that security, meet the proposed compact-size targets and measure runtimes for a stated message length. This optional benchmark would assess practical usefulness.

uncertain: Limits on particular proof methods leave open whether a different method can establish the general construction.
A theoretical construction might require keys, encrypted messages or running times too large for practical use.
Security against quantum computers does not follow from the stated assumptions and attacker model.

page.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
page.definition: A general construction turns any classical one-way function—efficient to compute but hard to invert on a uniformly random input—into public-key encryption, where anyone can encrypt with a published key and only the secret-key holder can decrypt. Security follows from one-wayness alone, using classical polynomial-time algorithms without an ideal random oracle or shared setup.

goal.need: The cited Merkle-style benchmark gives an eavesdropper roughly N² computation steps against N steps by the participants; its realization from one-way functions assumes exponential inversion hardness. Ordinary encryption requires security against every polynomial-time attacker. One-way functions already suffice for pseudorandom generators. Extending that implication to public-key encryption would put both capabilities on the same computational assumption.

statements.body: Applebaum, Barak and Wigderson, developers of public-key encryption constructions
statements.quote: A complete solution to this problem would be obtained by constructing public key encryption based solely on the existence of one-way functions.
statements.context: The problem is broadening the computational foundations of public-key encryption.

statements.body: Garg, Hajiabadi, Mahmoody and Mohammed, cryptographic construction and separation researchers

statements.context: The committee describes the mathematical structure used by existing public-key constructions; it does not set an OWF-only construction target.

completion.title: One-way functions imply public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attack.
completion.criterion: Prove a general construction from any classical one-way function, with classical probabilistic polynomial-time key generation, encryption and decryption, without additional hardness or setup assumptions. Decryption error is negligible. Given the public key and two chosen equal-length messages, every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary identifies the encrypted message with probability at most 1/2 + negl(n). Here n is the security parameter; negl(n) is eventually below n^−c for every c > 0. A non-negligible distinguishing attack must yield an efficient inverter. The construction and reduction may use code.
completion.set_by: Cryptographic community; Barak’s Lecture 10 states the desired implication and defines its chosen-plaintext security game. Håstad et al. establish equivalence of the pseudorandom-generator and one-way-function assumptions.
completion.threshold_quote: If the PRG assumption is true then there exists a CPA-secure public key encryption.
completion.basis: The published implication and CPA game specify the theoretical goal. A fixed quadratic work gap does not satisfy security against every polynomial-time attacker. Li, Ni and Zan’s 2023 construction claim is catalogued as a preprint. A separate preprint submitted on 28 September 2026 still describes Minicrypt assumptions as not known to imply public-key encryption.

milestones.title: Any one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator that stretches its seed by at least one bit.
milestones.criterion: From any one-way function, construct a polynomial-time generator G that maps an n-bit uniform seed to at least n+1 bits. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher, the acceptance-probability difference between G’s output and a uniform string of the same length is negligible in n. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby proved this implication; their journal article was published on 7 April 1999.
milestones.set_by: Cryptographic community; Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby, Definition 3.5 and Theorem 6.3.
milestones.threshold_quote: The definition of a pseudorandom generator only requires the generator to stretch the input by at least one bit.

milestones.title: A random-oracle key-agreement protocol achieves a quadratic oracle-query gap.
milestones.criterion: In the random-oracle model, honest parties use O(N) oracle queries to agree on a secret, while an eavesdropper making o(N²) queries recovers it with probability o(1). A random oracle is an ideal uniformly random function accessible to all parties. Merkle published the puzzle construction in 1978; Barak and Mahmoody-Ghidary give its oracle-query analysis and prove a matching quadratic upper bound. Query counts do not bound the attacker’s computation between queries.
milestones.set_by: Merkle’s published puzzle protocol; its random-oracle security benchmark is formalized by Barak and Mahmoody-Ghidary.
milestones.threshold_quote: work which increases as the square of the work required of the two communicants to select the key.

milestones.title: Key agreement from exponentially hard one-way functions attains a nearly quadratic time gap.
milestones.criterion: Assume a function on k-bit inputs cannot be inverted with probability above 2^(−αk) in time 2^(αk), where α ≥ 1/2 − δ and 0 < δ < 1/10 are constants. Obtain key agreement with honest-party running time N for which adversaries running in time at most N^(2−10δ) recover the secret with probability o(1). Biham, Goren and Ishai proved this in 2008; Barak and Mahmoody-Ghidary state these quantitative parameters. This assumes exponential hardness and gives a fixed polynomial time gap.
milestones.set_by: Biham, Goren and Ishai’s TCC 2008 protocol; quantitative parameters as stated by Barak and Mahmoody-Ghidary.
milestones.threshold_quote: a key agreement protocol resisting adversaries whose running time is nearly quadratic in the running time of the honest parties.

milestones.title: Key agreement from any one-way function resists every polynomial-time eavesdropper.
milestones.criterion: From an arbitrary classical one-way function alone, construct polynomial-time parties communicating classically over a public channel, without an ideal oracle or shared setup. Their n-bit outputs agree with probability 1 − negl(n); every probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdropper given the transcript recovers the first party’s output with probability at most negl(n). Ball et al. characterize the OWF-to-key-agreement question through a reduction between two promise problems. Interaction is allowed; obtaining public-key encryption remains a further step.
milestones.set_by: Cryptographic community; Ball, Liu, Mazor and Pass, Definition 2.11 and the stated OWF-to-key-agreement question. The security definition is independent of the underlying assumption.
milestones.threshold_quote: Such a protocol is a key-agreement protocol if it is a (1 − neg(n), neg(n))-key-agreement.

not_found: No government programme or standards-body document specifying an OWF-to-PKE completion test or staged roadmap was found.
No peer-reviewed validation of Li, Ni and Zan’s 2023 construction claim was found.
No OWF-only construction meeting the interactive key-agreement criterion was found in the located peer-reviewed literature.
The ACM page for the 1989 Impagliazzo–Rudich paper returned HTTP 403; its CRYPTO ’88 version was accessible through Springer.
